title: Why does ice float?
subtitle: Water & molecules
subject: sciences
description: Ice floats on water. It looks perfectly normal, but it is in fact very rare. And lucky for life on Earth.

hero.hook: If ice sank, lakes would freeze all the way down. And life in the water would struggle to survive.

blocks.text: An ice cube in a glass, an iceberg in the ocean: ice **floats**. It looks ordinary. Yet for most substances the solid form is **denser**, heavier for the same volume, so it sinks.
Water does the opposite. The exception comes from the shape of its molecule. And it has saved a great many lakes in winter.

sections.title: A molecule shaped like a V

blocks.text: A water molecule is one **oxygen** atom joined to two **hydrogen** atoms. It is not straight: it forms a **V**. Because of that shape, the electric charges are not spread evenly, so the molecule is **polar**, slightly negative at one end and slightly positive at the other.

blocks.caption: The water molecule: a V that pulls its neighbors in and pushes them away

blocks.text: The result: water molecules attract each other through [[hydrogen bonds]], like small magnets. In the liquid they stay close but keep moving. In ice they lock into place in a different pattern.

sections.title: Freezing water takes up more room

blocks.text: Around **0°C**, water turns solid. To build ice, the molecules line up in a **hexagonal** network, a kind of six-sided honeycomb. That leaves more **empty space** between them than in the liquid.
This is why a full water bottle can **burst** in the freezer: ice takes up more room than liquid water.

Less matter in the same volume means **less dense**. And anything less dense than the liquid around it rises. So ice floats on water. This is what we call the **anomalous expansion of water**: unlike almost every other substance, water expands as it cools below **4°C**.

blocks.caption: An iceberg floats because ice is less dense than liquid water

sections.title: Why this is vital for lakes

blocks.text: Imagine if ice sank. It would form at the surface, then drop to the bottom. The lake would freeze layer after layer, all the way down. Summer would often be too short to melt it all.

Luckily, ice stays on top. It works as an **insulating lid**. Under the frozen surface, the water can stay around **4°C**, the temperature at which liquid water is densest, warm enough for fish and water plants to survive.

White sea ice sends much of the Sun's light back into space thanks to its high **albedo**, its reflecting power. If the ice goes, the dark ocean soaks up more heat. That speeds up warming: a vicious circle.
Ice floats because, as it freezes, water builds a more open network and becomes less dense than liquid water. That one exception protects life in the water through the winter.
